tier_reason: lemire/zone_benchmarks README (harness benchmarks/bench.cpp + simdzonehelper.h, public) shows simdzone haswell 0.81 GB/s, westmere 0.73, fallback 0.38 vs knot3.3.4 0.19 GB/s on the 1361515551-byte se.zone.txt, but no CPU model and no exact compiler, so not A. The win is backed by the peer-reviewed paper (Koekkoek and Lemire, Software: Practice and Experience 55(4), 2025), whose reported figures (simdzone above 0.8 GB/s, Knot 0.19-0.32 GB/s, NSD 0.05-0.07 GB/s) were seen only in search snippets because arxiv.org and the TELUQ repository are blocked.

corrections.caveats: The quoted table is from the benchmark repo of Daniel Lemire, co-author of the simdzone paper (Koekkoek and Lemire, 'Parsing Millions of DNS Records per Second', Software: Practice and Experience 55(4), 2025; the simdzone README still says 'to appear'), so it is not independent of the project. The paper could not be opened (arxiv.org and r-libre.teluq.ca blocked); search snippets quote simdzone above 0.8 GB/s, Knot DNS at 0.19 to 0.32 GB/s and NSD's parser at 0.05 to 0.07 GB/s (snippet only). The README example output predates the current harness: it prints 'simdzonehaswell' and has no read_file or 'zonec (NSD 4.9)' rows, which bench.cpp now emits, so no published zonec number exists on the repo page. Build asymmetry: simdzone is fetched at commit aab6386 and built from source in CMake Release, while Knot's zscanner comes from Ubuntu 24.04's prebuilt libknot-dev package with distro flags. No CPU model or compiler version is given on reachable pages; the Dockerfile installs both g++ and clang and CMake picks the default. One zone file (.se) in the README; both parsers only count records in a callback rather than building a zone, and the timed region includes reading the file (expected to be in page cache). The simdzone repo README states no baseline comparison of its own (its i7-1065G7 .com run has no competitor). SIMD kernels are x86-64 only (SSE4.2, AVX2); other targets use the fallback kernel, which is about 2x Knot in this run (derived from page data).

notes: Numbers match the zone_benchmarks README exactly; harness is a real full parse with a counting callback on both sides (no no-op). Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause, 137 stars, 24 forks, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-30, active. Shortcomings to record: co-author's benchmark repo, CPU and compiler unstated, Knot from distro package vs simdzone built from source, paper seen via snippets only, x86-64-only SIMD.

tier_reason: Independent measurement by the fast-http author (fukamachi/fast-http README at commit 6b91103, the exact commit the picohttpparser README cites): picohttpparser 0.036571 s vs http-parser 0.289766 s for 100000 parses, with both bench.c programs inline, Apple clang-600.0.51 and -O3 stated, but the CPU is only '3GHz Intel Core i7', so not A. A second independent run (ioplane/iohttpparser, 2026, clang 22.1.0 Release+ThinLTO, generic KVM 'AMD EPYC Processor' vCPU) has picohttpparser ahead of llhttp 9.3.1 in all 21 common scenarios, also without a CPU SKU.

corrections.claimed_speedup: fukamachi/fast-http@6b91103 README, 100000 parses of one 430-byte GET request: picohttpparser 0.036571 s vs joyent http-parser 0.289766 s (table rounds it to 0.289s), about 7.9x (derived from page data). The same commit lists fast-http (Common Lisp) at 0.045 s; a later fast-http commit (copied in goobl/fast-http) revises fast-http to 0.138 s and says picohttpparser is '3.7 times faster' than fast-http, with the picohttpparser and http-parser times unchanged. Second independent source (ioplane/iohttpparser run 20260313T210231Z-3b9c398, summary.md, median req/s): picohttpparser beats llhttp 9.3.1 in all 21 common scenarios, 1.45x (hdr-count-16-minimal, 5.64M vs 3.88M) to 2.47x (hdr-value-heavy, 8.77M vs 3.55M), median about 1.9x; req-pico-bench 7.63M vs 3.21M (2.38x), req-headers 13.73M vs 7.87M (1.74x), and req-connect 23.55M vs 11.36M (2.07x) in the CONNECT table (all ratios derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: fast-http page: 'GCC version 6.0 (clang-600.0.51)' (Apple clang on OS X Mavericks), gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O3 for both bench.c programs, no -msse4.2 or -march, so picohttpparser's __SSE4_2__ path (if present in that 2014 revision) was compiled out and its scalar path ran. http_parser.o comes from 'make' in the http-parser repo; the 2014 Makefile (tag v2.3) builds it with -O3 -DHTTP_PARSER_STRICT=0. iohttpparser run: clang 22.1.0, CMake clang-release preset (Release, CMAKE_INTERPROCEDURAL_OPTIMIZATION=ON, -fuse-ld=lld -flto=thin); picohttpparser and llhttp compiled from vendored sources without -msse4.2.
corrections.license: MIT OR Perl License (Artistic-1.0-Perl OR GPL-1.0-or-later), stated in README and source-file headers; no separate LICENSE file
corrections.stars_or_usage: 2.1k stars, 276 forks; HTTP/1 parser of H2O; used by Perl modules Plack, Starman, Starlet and Furl
corrections.caveats: Primary numbers are from fukamachi/fast-http's README (2014), an independent author benchmarking his own Common Lisp parser; the record's original URL, goobl/fast-http, is a 0-star fork copying a later fast-http commit. The later commit's note says PicoHTTPParser was deleted from the chart 'because the benchmark was wrong'; since fast-http's own time moved from 0.045 s to 0.138 s while picohttpparser (0.036571 s) and http-parser (0.289766 s) stayed the same, the error appears to be in fast-http's row, but the note is ambiguous. The current fast-http README no longer has picohttpparser rows. Microbenchmark: one request repeated 100000 times (about 37 ms total), clock() into float, single run, 2014 hardware and Apple clang, CPU only '3GHz Intel Core i7'. The http-parser loop re-initializes the parser each iteration and uses null callbacks; the picohttpparser compile line reads 'gcc ... http_parser.c bench.c', a copy-paste slip. picohttpparser's SIMD path needs -msse4.2 at compile time (no runtime dispatch) and is x86 only; both third-party runs used its scalar path, so the wins are conservative. In the 2026 iohttpparser run, llhttp registers only on_message_complete while picohttpparser fills its header array, which also favours llhttp; the CPU is a generic KVM 'AMD EPYC Processor' vCPU. The picohttpparser README's own benchmark chart is a gyazo PNG (not readable here) and the repo's bench.c times picohttpparser alone (10 million parses). picohttpparser is itself a named baseline of the http-parsers category (spec Part 4: llhttp, http-parser, picohttpparser). The SSE4.2 path is often silently compiled out downstream (H2O's default CMake build, pico-sys), which several rival parsers' 'faster than picohttpparser' claims rely on. An unmerged AVX2 fork (vkrasnov/picohttpparser, 2014) is listed separately.

notes: Upstream h2o/picohttpparser is the canonical project, not a duplicate: vkrasnov/picohttpparser is an unmerged 2014 fork whose wave 5 claim is fork-vs-upstream (AVX2 path never merged), and picohttpparser-rs is a Rust port benchmarked against upstream; keep this record as the canonical entry and keep the fork as its own is_fork_of variant (if one record per project is wanted, the fork folds into this one, not the reverse). Metadata checked: not a fork, not archived, 2.1k stars, last commit 2026-09-29 (Atom feed), active. Shortcomings to record: 2014 single-run microbenchmark without CPU model, scalar path measured, ambiguous 'benchmark was wrong' note on the source page.

tier_reason: First-party README 'Performance' section shows the quoted jansson vs UCL parse and emit times exactly, with no CPU, compiler, versions or jansson build flags; the repo's tests/test_speed.c times UCL alone and no jansson harness is public, so the comparison is not reproducible: C.

corrections.caveats: First-party README numbers from one run on one generated 19 MB JSON file: no CPU, OS, compiler version, jansson version or jansson build flags are given, and the two UCL sets differ in optimization level (the first is unoptimized, the second -O3), so the ratios mix builds. tests/test_speed.c (2013 copyright header, so the numbers are probably old) times only UCL: it mmaps the file, uses UCL_PARSER_ZEROCOPY and times ucl_parser_add_chunk plus ucl_parser_get_object with clock_gettime; the jansson harness is not in the repo, and the README's 'make check' suggestion runs only UCL. Whether the quoted run used zero-copy is not said; zero-copy favours UCL over jansson, which allocates its own strings. The emit gap against jansson is small (about 1.1x for JSON). The only evidence is JSON parsing and emitting, not UCL's own config syntax or YAML/TOML/XML parsing against the category's baselines (libyaml, yaml-cpp, toml++, libxml2, pugixml). No independent benchmark including libucl was found.

notes: Numbers match the README verbatim; metadata checked: BSD-2-Clause (COPYING), 1.7k stars, 162 forks, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-04, active. Domain: the raw record carries domain parsing-and-text from the w3-mine-b assignment, but its category yaml-toml-xml belongs to serialization-and-formats, so record a domain override (domain is not a correction field here). Shortcomings to record: first-party one-run numbers, no jansson harness or flags, mixed optimization levels, JSON-only evidence.
